content.text:
The Child Who Runs Away at the Word 'Bath'

There's a tug-of-war that happens every evening. When you tell your child, who has been playing energetically all day, that it's bath time, they wriggle and squirm and run away. Hating water on their head and stinging eyes, they wear you out day after day.

In truth, it's natural for a child to dislike baths. Playtime being cut off all of a sudden, and the unfamiliar sensations, are a burden to a child. What matters is not the command 'you have to wash,' but a small shift that turns bath time into something worth looking forward to.

Curious about the story of kids who hate baths? Take a look at its lesson through pictures. Meet the key scenes of the tale too. Read it together with your child and talk about it. We've gathered many stories about toddler bath habits, bath habit storybooks, hygiene habit storybooks and more, all around 07. Splash-Splash, Bubble-Bubble!

content.alt: 07. Splash-Splash, Bubble-Bubble! - The Real Reason the Bath Habit Matters
content.text:
The Real Reason the Bath Habit Matters

A bath is more than simple cleanliness; it's a child's first experience of caring for their own body. By repeating the sense of washing when they sweat and feeling refreshed once they wash, a child learns the foundation of independence: 'I take care of my body.'

An evening bath also becomes a natural signal that wraps up the day and leads into sleep. Rather than forcing them to wash, helping a child feel that refreshed sensation for themselves turns a bath from something to reject into an everyday joy.
content.caption: When they feel the freshness for themselves, a bath becomes play.

content.alt: 07. Splash-Splash, Bubble-Bubble! - Hori's Great Bubble Land Adventure Story
content.text:
Hori's Great Bubble Land Adventure Story

Hori, the hero of "Splash-Splash, Bubble-Bubble!", also hates baths at first and runs off to the living room with a towel over his head. But sitting on the sofa, his sticky, itchy body feels so uncomfortable.

Just then, Dad holds out his hand with a sponge and bath toys and asks, 'Shall we go on a Great Bubble Land Adventure?' White bubbles swell up like a mountain in the tub, hair-washing becomes a waterfall, soaping up becomes a snowman, and rinsing becomes a sparkle game. After finishing the adventure, Hori is amazed at his soft, dry body and laughs, 'Baths were this much fun?'
content.caption: Dad's one line turned bath time into an 'adventure game.'

content.alt: 07. Splash-Splash, Bubble-Bubble! - Let's Practice Together at Home
content.text:
Let's Practice Together at Home

After reading the book, connect the story to actual bath time. First, before the bath, chant the refrain 'splash-splash, bubble-bubble' together to build a sense of anticipation.

Second, give hair-washing, soaping up, and rinsing names like waterfall, snowman, and sparkle to turn them into a step-by-step game. When your child can predict the next step, they feel less anxious. Third, when the bath is over, name the freshness out loud by asking 'feels refreshing, right?', and that feeling will make them look forward to the next bath.
content.caption: Name the fresh feeling out loud after the bath.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How do I soothe a child who hates baths?

A. Help them feel it as splashy, exciting play rather than something to fear about the water. Adding their favorite bath toys and playing with bubbles turns bath time into a time they look forward to.

Q. Is there a way to make baths feel like play?

A. Make shapes out of bubbles or splash the water while chatting together. Even a child who hates baths wants to wash themselves within a fun imaginative game.

Q. My child especially hates having their hair washed.

A. Many are afraid water will get in their eyes, so reassure them with a game of tilting the head back. Praising them warmly when they endure it well helps them relax little by little.
